Chapter Three: Disciples (Fascicle 2b–2e). Regarding the "Chapter on Disciples": within this chapter, the voice of the Śrāvaka disciples is commissioned to inquire after the illness [of the Buddha].

It is because the study of the Śrāvakas follows that of the Buddha that they are called "disciples" (*dizi*); and because they are born through transformation from the Buddha, they are further termed [disciples].
My son,
based on what was thus declared, the chapter title is named "The Chapter on Disciples.
Next, the text will be explained according to its passages.
Within this, a brief analysis is presented by way of three sections:
first, explaining the purpose of its introduction in relation to what precedes it;
second, relating it to the subsequent structural divisions.
Third, the correct interpretation according to the text.
How is the purpose of its arrival [in this treatise] to be understood?
This is explained through two points:
First, the purpose of its arrival is explained by way of the introductory section; second, the purpose is interpreted in relation to the main body of the text.
Regarding the explanation by way of the introduction, there are further two parts:
first, the explanation in terms of the Buddha.

In the preceding chapter, Vimalakīrti manifested illness as an occasion for instruction; his manifestation of illness was intended to prompt the teaching. Since he required the Buddha’s influence, from this point onward, the Tathāgata initiates the discourse by posing questions to provoke his explanation.
Regarding the person to whom this was addressed: it was first addressed to the Śrāvakas, which is why this chapter follows.
Second, it is explained by manifesting the virtues of Vimalakīrti.

At the beginning of the preceding chapter, his virtues were directly extolled and manifested; at the end of that chapter, his virtues were manifested through a parable. These two instances are termed "manifesting virtues through transformative manifestation."
From this point onward, the text proceeds by means of analogies to manifest its virtues; first, it manifests their high virtue in contrast to the Śrāvakas, which is why this chapter follows.
Such is the explanation regarding the introduction.

To explain the purpose of its arrival according to the main body of the text: in the preceding chapter, because of the inquiry into illness by ordinary beings, the teaching for ordinary beings was clarified, proceeding from the ordinary to the holy.
From this point onward, based on the Illustrious One’s inquiry regarding illness, the teaching of the noble Dharma is clarified.
Within these noble teachings, the Śrāvakas are taught first; therefore, this chapter follows.
Such is the purpose of its arrival.
Next, I shall analyze the text.
This section contains two parts:
first, the structural analysis according to the introduction.
From this point until the passage "sleeping alone on a single bed because of his illness," the text is divided into three parts:
first, Vimalakīrti’s thought that prompts the inquiry;
second, the Tathāgata’s response to that thought by commanding an inquiry into his illness.
3. Vimalakīrti contemplates Mañjuśrī and his retinue descending; he awaits their questions in an empty room.
2. Regarding the main body of the text, its structure is analyzed as follows:
from this point until the end of the "Gandhavyūha" (Incense Accumulation) chapter, the text is divided into two parts.
I. Vimalakīrti reflects upon awaiting the holy inquiry;
II. From "The Buddha knows" onwards, the Tathāgata provides the inquiry to reveal what he has taught.
The topical divisions are thus.
Next, I shall explain the text.
First, I will interpret the initial section concerning Vimalakīrti’s thought.
The phrase "at that time" refers to the moment when the thought arose.
"Vimalakīrti, the Elder," refers to the person who gave rise to the thought.
"He himself reflected upon his illness," and so forth, indicates that he was precisely generating this state of mind.

However, in this passage, the thought awaits the inquiry of a sage; it is not that he is thinking about his own disease. This is because Vimalakīrti’s compassion for sentient beings is profound, and his longing for their transformation is like thirst; thus, he gave rise to this reflection.

Vimalakīrti manifested illness solely out of concern for sentient beings; yet, although his mind was directed toward others, the work of transformation could only be accomplished through the influence of a Buddha. Therefore, he thought to himself: "I lie ill upon my bed; will the World-Honored One, in his great compassion, not deign to show me mercy?"
Since illness is the object of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one contemplates oneself lying ill upon the bed.
Since only the Buddha pities suffering, one contemplates the World-Honored One.
Since the Buddha possesses profound compassion and feels great pity for those in pain, one contemplates Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

He invokes the Buddha’s great compassion, desiring that the Tathāgata take pity on his own suffering from illness and have mercy upon those he has transformed; thus, for his own sake, he must certainly inquire.
Since one who possesses great compassion ought to show pity when seeing such a state, he further wonders and laments why [the Buddha] does not extend his compassion.
"Nei" means "peaceful.
I am currently suffering from illness; how could you remain at peace while enduring this and fail to show me compassion?
To feel pity in one's heart is not what is meant by "showing compassion" (chui-min).
"Compassion" refers to pity and sympathy.
The Buddha, perceiving their thoughts, dispatched someone to inquire about them.
"The Buddha knew their intent," he said, explaining the reason for his arising.

First, to manifest that the Tathāgata’s mind is impartial and non-biased, he makes this public announcement.
This is similar to how, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he universally addresses the great assembly and invites them to inquire.
The second reason is that, wishing to extensively entrust these words to the assembly to manifest the virtues of Vimalakīrti, it was necessary to issue a general summons.
Summoning those who were deemed incapable served to reveal the loftiness of his virtue;
summoning those who were deemed capable served to manifest the subtlety of his virtue.
The third reason is that, wishing to extensively entrust these words to others in order to manifest the Dharma taught by Vimalakīrti, it is necessary to issue a general proclamation.
Therefore, in the following text, he first informs those who are unfit to reveal what was previously taught, and subsequently informs those who are fit to clarify what is being taught now.
These are general announcements. For what reason are those who are incapable announced first, followed by those who are capable?
There are two interpretations:

first, it is because one wishes to announce them in sequence so that they may inquire, thereby fulfilling the three aforementioned points; for this reason, those who are incapable are announced first.
If one has first announced that [the assembly] is capable, it would be inappropriate to subsequently announce that they are incapable.

The second reason for doing so is the desire to contrast the incapacity with the subsequent manifestation of capability; since the person being questioned is eminent and what is taught will necessarily be profound, this inspires a sense of longing and aspiration in others. For this reason, one first announces that they are incapable.
Regarding the announcement concerning those who are incapable, he first announces it to the śrāvakas and subsequently to the bodhisattvas.
Since the Tathāgata is already fully aware that the śrāvakas are incapable, why would he take the trouble to announce it to them?
There are three ways of understanding this:
First, it is to manifest the equality of the Buddha’s mind, similar to how in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* he first instructed the bhikṣus to ask questions.
Second, it is because he wished to extensively demonstrate Vimalakīrti’s virtues before the assembly; therefore, he had to announce it to all.
Therefore, in the subsequent text, he first addresses the śrāvakas to demonstrate that Vimalakīrti’s virtue is superior and transcends those of the two vehicles;
subsequently, he addresses the bodhisattvas to demonstrate that Vimalakīrti’s virtue surpasses that of all bodhisattvas.
Third, because he wishes to extensively entrust these words to manifest the Dharma taught by Vimalakīrti, it is necessary to issue a general announcement.
Therefore, in the following text, he first addresses the śrāvakas to clarify the teaching he expounds for the śrāvakas;
subsequently, he addresses the bodhisattvas to clarify the teaching he expounds for the bodhisattvas.
This is a general announcement. For what reason is the Śrāvaka addressed first and the Bodhisattva addressed later?
There are three interpretations:
first, the Śrāvaka is close to the Buddha; being close, he is addressed first.
It is not so for the Bodhisattvas; this is stated later.
Second, it is intended that the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas be informed and prompted to inquire, thereby fulfilling the three preceding meanings. For this reason, the Śrāvakas are addressed first.
If the Tathāgata were to address the Bodhisattvas first, it would then be inappropriate to address the Śrāvakas later, as they are inferior.

The third meaning concerns the sequential order of the teachings. In the preceding chapter, it was clarified that the teachings for ordinary beings proceed from the ordinary to the holy; therefore, in this chapter, he next addresses the śrāvakas to contrast them and manifest the teaching of the śrāvaka-dharma, which proceeds from the small to the great. Consequently, it is only in the subsequent chapter that he addresses the bodhisattvas, contrasting them to manifest the bodhisattva-dharma; such is the proper sequence of the transformative teachings.
Within this chapter, there are five hundred śrāvakas addressed; the first ten are listed individually, while the remainder are cited collectively.
Among the first ten, the causes of the dharmakāya are elucidated in relation to the first nine persons, and the fruit of the dharmakāya is elucidated in relation to the final one.
Within the preceding nine [categories], the method of cultivation is clarified for the first eight persons, while the method of renunciation is clarified for the final one.
Within the first eight, the cultivation of wholesome dharmas is clarified for the first seven persons, while the cessation of unwholesome dharmas is manifested for the final one.

Within the preceding seven [categories], the practice of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is elucidated in relation to the first six persons, while the arising of the path of penetration (*prativedhamārga*) is elucidated in relation to the final one.
The essence of the path of cultivation is the body, and the arising of the path of penetration is its function.

Within the first six [sections], Śāriputra first elucidates the practice of non-abiding; next, in response to Maudgalyāyana, he elucidates the practice of entering realization; and in response to the final four [disciples], he elucidates the practice of the aids to the path.
This refers to the three paths of common characteristics (*sādharmya*) as presented in the *Bhūmi-sūtra*.
Within the first of these, regarding human beings, there is first the command and subsequently the departure.
"He commanded Śāriputra, 'Go and inquire after his illness,'" is the command.

The name Śāriputra has already been explained above. He was the son of a brāhmaṇa from Rājagṛha; his father was originally a man from South India, while his maternal grandfather was a great master of debate in Rājagṛha who had been granted a fief by the king.
When Śāriputra’s father arrived, he engaged in debate with him; the maternal grandfather was defeated, and the King confiscated his fief and bestowed it upon Śāriputra’s father.
Consequently, the grandfather married his daughter to him, and they begot Śāriputra.
Regarding Śāriputra’s mother, she had previously engaged in debate with her elder brother Mahākoṭṭhila, but she was always inferior to him;
however, once she conceived Śāriputra, she consistently gained the upper hand in debate, leading Koṭṭhila to study even more diligently in order to surpass her.
In a later birth, Śāriputra was seven years old when he became the foremost in debate among the sixteen kingdoms.
Later, when the Buddha appeared in the world, he followed the Buddha and left the household life, becoming the foremost in wisdom among the Buddha’s disciples.

Therefore, other treatises praise the śarīra, stating that if one were to compare the wisdom and learning of all classes of beings with that of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, alone, they could not equal even a sixteenth part of it.
I shall inform him first.
Why inform him first?
Because he is preeminent among the disciples for his superior wisdom; it is for this reason that I inform him first.
Question: It was previously stated that the Buddha spoke first to the śrāvakas because their virtues were inferior.
Since Śāriputra is the most excellent among the disciples, why did the Buddha speak to him first?
The commentary states:

Although Śāriputra’s practice of wisdom is superior, his other practices are inferior to those of others; therefore, he was addressed later. This is because each of the śrāvakas possesses their own foremost and most excellent quality.
"I am not capable," and so forth, are words of refusal.
Within this, there is first the refusal, next the explanation, and finally the conclusion.
"I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness" constitutes the initial refusal.
The section beginning with "Therefore" provides the explanation;
the section beginning with "Thus I" provides the conclusion.
Within the explanation, the phrase "for what reason" serves as a self-interrogation, which introduces the subsequent statement: "What grounds do I have to say that I am incapable?"
The following provides the formal explanation.
Previously, he was rebuked for being incapable;
herein, first the causal conditions for that rebuke are set forth.
"Then Vimalakīrti," and so forth, records the words spoken in response to the reprimand.
"Then I, World-Honored One, having heard these words," and so forth, reveals his own inadequacy by acknowledging his own lowliness and deficiencies.
At the beginning, "recalling the past" introduces the time when he was rebuked;
"once in the forest" identifies the place where he was rebuked;
and "sitting in meditation beneath a tree" clarifies the specific incident for which he was rebuked.
"Yan" (宴) is synonymous with "mo" (默).
Sitting silently beneath a tree is called "yan-za" (宴坐).
"Yan" and "yan" (晏) mutually oversee one another.
"Yan" has the meaning of peace (*āśvasta*), while "yan" has the meaning of silence (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*); they are entirely distinct, yet here "yan" is made manifest.
Below follows the words of reproach.
The reason it is necessary to reproach [him] is to cause Śāriputra to abandon the minor and take up the major, and to benefit others as well.
Within this, the initial statement, "Vimalakīrti came and said," serves as a general heading.
The specific details of his address and title are not individually revealed here.
First he rebukes, and subsequently he instructs.
The statement, “Śāriputra, it is not necessarily sitting in this manner that constitutes ‘sitting in dhyāna,’” is a word of censure.
“Only” (唯) is a term of respect.
Śāriputra has left the household life, whereas Vimalakīrti remains in the secular world; since those in the secular world must show respect toward the Path, he uses the word “only.”
The same applies to all subsequent sections.
Since the superior seat has not yet been manifested, it cannot be entirely rejected; therefore, it is said that it is "not necessarily" so.
Below, the scriptural words are presented, which first introduce the subject, then provide the instruction, and finally offer praise.
"Regarding 'one who sits in meditative composure' (yañ-źa-ba), this is a general heading.
The word 'regarding' (fu) serves as the opening of the discourse.
This introduces the method of the Bodhisattva’s superior sitting."
The following provides a detailed explanation, which consists of six phrases organized into four groups:
the first phrase constitutes one group, teaching the departure from ordinary conduct, the relinquishing of marks, and the realization of tranquility;
the next two phrases constitute another group, teaching the departure from Hinayana conduct, the arising of function from within tranquility, and remaining pure while constantly amidst defilement.
Next, one [phrase] constitutes a single unit, emphasizing the teaching on transcending ordinary beings by abandoning the realization of quiescence;
the latter two [phrases] constitute another unit, emphasizing the teaching on transcending conditioned practice by remaining eternally pure while amidst defilement.
Regarding the first phrase, "not manifesting body or mind within the three realms," the desire, form, and formless realms are these three realms.
Ordinary beings dwelling in the two realms of desire and form receive the fruit of physical form, which is called the "manifest body";
dwelling in the formless realm, they receive the fruit of mind and mental factors, which is termed the "manifest mind."

The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that the three realms are illusory and are merely the products of the mind; having realized this truth, he abandons them, finding no place where they exist. For this reason, he does not manifest body or mind within the stages of the three realms; this is the summary.

In the following two phrases, the first phrase indicates that based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one arises in activity from within stillness; the second phrase indicates that based on wisdom (*prajñā*), one remains in purity yet is constantly engaged with defilement.

Regarding the first phrase, "not arising from the extinction samādhi while manifesting dignified deportment," the "extinction samādhi" refers to the *nirodha-samāpatti* among the nine successive attainments.
The cessation of mental perception is called the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodhasamāpatti*); its meaning is as explained in a separate chapter and should be discussed in full there.
"Postures" refers to the four postures: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are the four postures.
The śrāvaka’s meditative absorption of cessation relinquishes the four modes of deportment;
the bodhisattva constantly manifests them. Why is this so?

The deportment (*īryāpatha*) of the śrāvaka arises from the mind of phenomenal consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*); when entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the mind of phenomenal consciousness ceases, and thus they relinquish their deportment.
There are three points of origin for the deportment of a bodhisattva: first, it arises based on the mind of phenomenal consciousness;

second, it arises based on the mind of deluded consciousness (*mṛṣā-vijñāna*); and finally, it arises based on the mind of true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*). It manifests spontaneously through the power of the dharma-gate of *yathābhūta-samādhi*, just as a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) can rain down precious objects without the mind engaging in conceptual discrimination.
Among the three types of mind, the first two are impermanent and can be extinguished by the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);
the latter one is a permanent mind and cannot be extinguished by the absorption of cessation.
That which is extinguished does not manifest bodily postures (*īryāpatha*) during the time of the absorption of cessation.
As for that which does not cease, although one remains in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one constantly manifests dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
Now, based on this latter meaning, he instructs Śāriputra; therefore, it is said that "without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation, one manifests dignified deportment."

Regarding the phrase "not abandoning the dharmas of the Path while manifesting ordinary affairs": noble wisdom is the Path, whereas afflictions, karma, and so forth are the affairs of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
While a *śrāvaka* is on the Path, they abandon the affairs of ordinary persons.
The Bodhisattva is constantly manifest.

Why is this so? Because those who are Śrāvakas have not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena; they perceive afflictions and the like as existing and thus fearsome, and having severed them, they enter the state of a noble one. Therefore, once they have attained the state of a noble one, they are unable to manifest [these afflictions].

The Bodhisattva exhaustively investigates emptiness and knows that existence is like an illusion; thus, though dwelling within it, he feels no fear. Consequently, he constantly practices the gathering and transformation of sentient beings, which is why he does not abandon them.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Practicing what is not the path serves to penetrate the Buddha-way."

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva realizes and enters the dharma-gate of the samādhi of dependent origination, by the power of this dharma-gate, they naturally manifest universally in common activities with ordinary beings.
This is precisely what is meant in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* when it says, "The Great Parinirvāṇa is able to establish the great purpose. This refers to that very matter.
Śrāvakas have not yet attained this Dharma, which is why they are unable [to do so].
Regarding the next phrase, "sitting in meditation with the mind dwelling neither within nor without": the six sense faculties are "within" and the six sense objects are called "without."
The mind-consciousness of ordinary beings arises with the six sense organs as its dominant condition; this is called "abiding within.
It arises with the six sense objects as its objective condition; this is said to be "outside."

The Bodhisattva is not like this; he knows that the deluded mind arises from the interaction of the faculties and their objects, just as there are faculties in a dream and objects in a dream. Since there is no phenomenon apart from the mind, and because he knows they do not exist, he remains detached and does not give rise to them. No longer relying on these to aggregate and produce consciousness, he dwells neither within nor without.
Therefore, the text below states: "Without mindfulness of internal or external [objects], one acts in equanimity.

Furthermore, the deluded mind is an impermanent phenomenon; when the six consciousnesses arise together, the initial arising consciousness must have a basis upon which it relies. That which is relied upon is termed the "root" (*indriya*) when it is predominant, and the "object" (*viṣaya*) when it is subordinate.
The true mind is eternally abiding and has nothing upon which to rely; because it is without reliance, one cannot speak of strong faculties or weak objects.
Now, I teach Śāriputra to abandon the false and grasp the true; therefore, not dwelling within nor being outside is what constitutes "sitting in meditation."

Regarding the latter two phrases: the first phrase clarifies that one practices the Noble Path while the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are currently manifest; the second phrase clarifies that one realizes *nirvāṇa* while the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are currently manifest.

Regarding the first sentence, "To practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment while remaining unmoved by various views is to sit in meditation": the mind characterized by the five views is called "various views"; these five are the view of a self, the view of extremes, false views, attachment to precepts and rituals, and attachment to views.
The Bodhisattva constantly manifests as transcending those whom he transforms according to their needs; this is called "immovability" because he never departs from them.

Therefore, the text below states: "There are eighty-four thousand gateways of afflictions through which sentient beings become exhausted, yet it is by means of these that the Buddhas perform the work of a Buddha."
"Although they manifest [defilements], their inner minds remain constantly stilled; therefore, they always cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Regarding 'entering nirvana without severing afflictions': it is called 'not severing' because they manifest greed, anger, ignorance, and so forth in accordance with their transformative teachings."
The constant tranquility of the inner mind is called entering nirvana.
This serves as the conclusion.
Because these various practices can only be accomplished through what is difficult to express, they are termed "quietude" (yan).
The place where the Sages dwell is called "sitting.
The above constitutes the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*).
"If one can thus" refers to what is approved; it praises excellence and exhorts one to study.
The Master raised his voice in reproach:
"At that time, O World-Honored One, having heard these words, I remained silent and was unable to offer a reply. Thus he expressed his own lowliness and deficiency, manifesting his own inadequacy.
This phrasing conforms to the linguistic conventions of foreign (Indic) languages; according to these, one should say: "World-Honored One!
When I heard this at that time, I remained silent and was unable to offer a reply.
This is the initial statement, followed by its explanation.
"Therefore, I am not fit for this," he concluded, expressing his own inability.
He then instructed Maudgalyāyana to go inquire after his illness.
Maudgalyāyana’s personal name was Kolita.
The father had previously been childless; he obtained [the boy] from the tree deity of the Kūṭadanta tree and gave him the name Kūṭadanta.

He was the son of a minister in Rājagṛha. Previously, he had practiced together with Śāriputra under Nātha, focusing his mind exclusively on seeking the Way but attaining nothing, leading him to claim that there was no Way.
As he was nearing the end of his life, he sighed faintly amidst his illness.
The two men asked him,
"Master, what are you sighing about?"
Nanda replied: "I recall that among the people of the world, beings are bound by affectionate attachment.
For instance, when the King of Suvarṇabhūmi in South India passed away and was cremated, his queen, out of longing and remembrance for him, threw herself into the fire and died."
"I sigh for this.
The two men recorded this in private.
Later, after Nātha had died, some merchants arrived from Suvarṇabhūmi; when the two men questioned them, it was just as Nātha had said.
The two men then said, "Our teacher has certainly attained the Way, but we ourselves are not human beings.
They subsequently made a pact:
"If either of us attains anything, we must inform the other."
After this vow had been made, the Buddha finally appeared in the world.
When the bhikṣu Aśvajit entered the city to beg for alms, Śāriputra observed that his deportment was extraordinary and knew that he possessed a superior teacher.
While waiting for him to return from begging alms, Śāriputra asked,
"Who is your teacher? Upatiṣya replied:
"This is a great śramaṇa," he said,
and asked again,
"What does your great śramaṇa proclaim?"
Aṅgīrasa replied:
"The Great Śramaṇa has taught that all phenomena arise through causes and conditions;
the Great Śramaṇa has taught that all phenomena cease through causes and conditions."
When Śāriputra questioned him, he attained sudden and complete awakening; at that very moment, he realized the first fruit of the path.
Upon returning to his own place, Maudgalyāyana saw him from afar and immediately knew that he had attained realization, so he went to question him.
Śāriputra replied in full detail according to what he had heard, and upon hearing this, Maudgalyāyana also attained the first fruit of enlightenment.
The two men subsequently joined the Buddha and left the household life; their respective followers followed them to the Buddha’s presence, and all together attained arhatship.
Among the Buddha’s disciples, Maudgalyāyana is foremost in supernormal powers; he is now commanded to inquire after [the Buddha’s] illness.
Within this passage, there is first an announcement, followed by a refusal of the task.
The refusal begins with a general statement, the section beginning with "The reason why" provides the explanation, and the section beginning with "Therefore" offers the conclusion.
First, there is a general understanding; following the self-interrogation within the explanation of the reason, the actual analysis and explanation follow.
This section contains four parts:
first, citing the circumstances of one's own past being rebuked.
1. "At that time, Vimalakīrti... and following, reveals the words of the reprimand; 2.
"When this Dharma was being taught, eight hundred residents of Vaiśālī set forth toward Bodhi... and following, shows the benefit of the reprimand; 3.
"I have no such eloquence," is a personal admission of inferiority, demonstrating that [Vimalakīrti's] skill is beyond reach.
At the beginning, "recalling the past" refers to the time he was rebuked.
"Entering Vaiśālī among the lanes and alleys" indicates the place where he was rebuked.
"Speaking for the sake of the laypeople" recounts the matter of the rebuke.
What kind of Dharma was he teaching?

Since this is not clarified in the text, it must have been for those lay householders that he taught the precepts, the giving of alms, and the dharma for rebirth in heaven; therefore, he was subsequently rebuked.
From here on is the second section, clarifying the words of admonition.
Why was this necessary?
It was for the benefit of Maudgalyāyana and the various lay devotees that he thus provided admonition.
In the text, "Vimalakīrti came and said" is the general statement;
that which follows "only" (唯) is the specific exposition.
Within the specific exposition, "it should not be as you, O worthy one, have said" is a word of censure.
Because the teaching does not accord with the Dharma, it is called "inappropriate" (budang).
Furthermore, because it does not accord with the capacities of the listeners, it is also inappropriate.
In the section following "preaching the Dharma," he instructs on how to preach correctly.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, teaching by way of the essence of the Dharma being taught;
second, from the passage "Now, one who preaches the Dharma neither speaks nor demonstrates" onwards, teaching by way of the manner of the preacher.
The preceding section extensively elucidates the characteristics of the Dharma-jewel to enable people to realize and enter it.
Within this, the first part provides a general overview, stating that "the Dharma is non-existent" without further distinction.
The subsequent section, beginning with "The nature of phenomena is thus; how could it be spoken," employs both reasoning and reductio ad absurdum.
Within the first general section, "Now, as for those who preach the Dharma" is a general mention of the act of preaching;
"they should preach in accordance with the Dharma" is a general exhortation to teach, meaning they should preach in accordance with the essential nature of the Jewel of the Dharma.
Below the phrase "the non-arising of dharmas," there follows the specific teaching according to the dharma.
Within this, the essence and characteristics of the Jewel of Dharma are extensively revealed so that one may rely upon its exposition.
Regarding the essence and characteristics of the Jewel of Dharma, it is as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* within the section on "Mindfulness of the Dharma":
Subtle, quiescent, and free from marks, it perfectly embodies all meanings; it is the sphere traversed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, eternal and unchanging.
This is precisely what is referred to in the sutras as the Buddha-nature, the True Dharma, and the Tathāgatagarbha.

The *tathatā* (suchness) is the true nature of all phenomena; within this true nature, there are no characteristics of phenomena. Therefore, in this passage, characteristics are refuted to reveal it, proclaiming that there is neither arising nor any phenomena whatsoever.

Although these words speak of emptiness, they are distinguished according to reality; therefore, throughout the following text, all explanations regarding the nature of phenomena state that there is no sentient being and no life-span, and so forth.

Yet, the Dharma is empty and harmonious, its meaning being omnipresent; for now, this is expounded by way of the five aggregates and the eighteen realms, while other categories may be understood by analogy.
First, regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), it clarifies that phenomena are devoid of characteristics and that phenomena lack "mine-ness" (*amama*).
Following the section on "being devoid of mine-ness," it clarifies that phenomena are devoid of characteristics by means of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).
Sentient beings frequently give rise to conceptual attachments regarding this subject; therefore, it is discussed here.
Within the first five aggregates (*skandhas*), there are ten distinct phrases, which clarify two meanings:
the first four phrases elucidate the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), while the latter six phrases elucidate the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
The meaning of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*) is explained extensively in a separate chapter and should be discussed in full here.
Within the context of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), how are the four propositions distinguished?

The first proposition clarifies that within the true dharma-body there is no sentient being; the second is "no-self" (*anātman*); the third is "no-life-force" (*ajīva*); and the fourth is "no-person" (*apudgala*).
This is precisely what is meant by the four meanings—non-self, non-sentient being, non-life-force, and non-person—in the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* regarding the Tathāgatagarbha.
In what way do these four, such as "self" and "sentient being," differ, that they must be separately refuted?
To provide a general explanation of a single entity is like having eyes; within it, when distinguished in detail, there are indeed differences.
What are these distinct characteristics?
To proclaim the substance of the aggregates (*skandha*) as the sovereign master and name it the "self" (*ātman*).
Within the combination [of aggregates], one calculates that there is a fixed reality and designates it as a "sentient being.
Within the continuity [of existence], one calculates that there is a divine nature that maintains and persists without interruption, which is called "life-span."
Within the midst of functional activity, there exists a sovereign controller; this is what is called the "person" (*pudgala*).
In contrast to that, one speaks of non-self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span.

Thus, the *Strīvivartavyūha-sūtra* states: "One contemplates that internally there is no self, externally there is no sentient being, and in the union of the internal and external there is no life-span; it is ultimately pure."
The reason there is no person is that, when observing within, one finds no self; the substance of the aggregates (skandhas) is not a spirit.

Without a producer externally, it is the collective functioning of the five aggregates that, when viewed in relation to their substantial body, is termed "external. Since there is no reality therein, it is called "no sentient being."

The union of the internal and external is devoid of a life-span; the aggregates arise together through designation, and this continuity is called "life. There is no separate essence of life, which is ultimately pure.
It is called "no person" because a person is designated by their governing function; since there is no essence of a self, the function of a person likewise does not exist, being ultimately pure.

In the text, the initial statement "Dharmas have no sentient beings" precisely clarifies that they lack existence in principle; that is, within the essence of the true Dharma-jewel, there are no sentient beings.
There are three kinds of non-existence:
first, the absence of a falsely imputed self or sentient being.
Second, among conventionally designated sentient beings, there is no fixed nature;
third, there is no characteristic of conventionally designated sentient beings.
These are all the existence of conceptual marks; therefore, they are entirely non-existent, and other functions are likewise so.
Regarding "free from the defilement of birth": this sentiment reveals the principle.
The mind that grasps at a self is called the "defilement of sentient beings";
within the true Dharma, there is no such mind of self, which is called being "free from the defilement of birth."
Because of the stainless mind, there are no sentient beings.
In the second phrase, "the selflessness of phenomena" (dharmanairātmya), it correctly clarifies the absence of principle.
Furthermore, within the true Dharma, the three kinds of self do not exist; this may be understood by analogy with what preceded.
Regarding "free from the defilement of self," this refers to destroying emotional attachments to reveal the principle; its meaning is the same as the previous explanation.
One should note that within these two phrases, emotional attachments are destroyed to reveal the principle, whereas in the latter two phrases, phenomenal marks are destroyed to reveal the principle.

In the third phrase, "Dharmas have no life-span," it correctly clarifies that there is no principle [of life]; likewise, within the true Dharma, the three kinds of life-span do not exist, which may be understood by analogy with what preceded.
Regarding the phrase "transcending birth and death," this destroys appearances to reveal the principle.
If birth and death truly existed within the Real Dharma, one could speak of a lifespan based upon them;
since birth and death do not exist, on what basis could one speak of a lifespan?

In the fourth phrase, "the person does not exist in the dharma," this correctly clarifies that there is no principle [of a person]; likewise, within the true dharma, the three types of persons do not exist, which may be understood by analogy with what preceded.
"Severing the past and future limits" destroys appearances to reveal the principle.
Conditioned phenomena arise in succession; the preceding is the "past limit" (pūrvānta) and the succeeding is the "future limit" (aparānta).
If these two limits existed within the true Dharma, one could then rely upon them to speak of persons;
since they do not exist within the truth, upon what could one speak of persons?

While they appear to exist from the perspective of conventional sentiment, they are fundamentally non-existent according to principle. It is by overturning sentiment to reveal principle that they are said to be "severed," rather than because there is something to be eliminated.

Regarding the clarification of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmasūnyatā) within the final six phrases: the first two are free from characteristics; the next two are free from names; the following single phrase concludes the preceding freedom from characteristics; and the final phrase concludes the aforementioned freedom from names.
In the first two phrases, the former phrase correctly clarifies the departure from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The latter phrase refutes the mental objects (*ālambana*) to establish the aforementioned departure from characteristics.
Within the first phrase, "The Dharma is eternally quiescent" correctly clarifies that the principle is non-existent.
Because the true Dharma is immovable, it is called "quiescent.
As for "extinguishing all dharmas," this means destroying marks to reveal quiescence.
The five aggregates are marks; since they are fundamentally non-existent within the truth, this is termed "extinguishing all marks."
That which possesses marks is not quiescent; because they are non-existent, it is quiescent.
Within the latter phrase, "dharmas are free from marks," this precisely clarifies that there is no [intrinsic] principle.
Within the true Dharma, there are no marks of the five aggregates; this is called "dharmas being free from marks."
"Non-objectification" means destroying appearances to reveal the principle.
If there were any appearance within this reality that could be taken as an object, it would not be called "free from appearances.
Since within the true dharma there is no appearance that can be taken as an object, the dharma is free from appearances.
Because there is no object of cognition, the cognizing subject is likewise non-existent.
In the subsequent two phrases, the first phrase refutes names and verbal designations, while the second phrase refutes mental perception to establish the previously mentioned detachment from speech.

Regarding the first phrase, "dharmas have no names," this correctly clarifies that reality is nameless; that is to say, within the true Dharma, there are no names established by those false conceptualizations.
Regarding "the severance of speech": it means destroying verbal expression to manifest the state of namelessness.
Since names are the basis of speech, when there is no name, speech does not arise; thus, it is called the "severance of speech."
When speech is raised, it is severed; thus, the establishment of names ceases.
Within the subsequent phrase, "Dharmas are beyond verbal expression because they are free from applied and sustained thought," the passions are refuted to reveal the principle.

Vitarka (initial application) and vicāra (sustained application) are said to be the causes of speech; because vitarka and vicāra do not exist within the true Dharma, speech does not arise, and thus there is no verbal expression.
Gross thought is termed vitarka, while the reception of thought is called vicāra; these both pertain to the realm of refinement.
Since the true Dharma transcends the realm of mental constructs, it is devoid of vitarka and vicāra.
The next line concludes the preceding discussion on the absence of characteristics:
"Dharmas have no form or appearance" correctly establishes that principle is non-existent, meaning that within the true Dharma there are no aggregates (*skandha*) or formal appearances.
By means of this, the preceding meaning of being free from marks is concluded; therefore, it is said to be "markless.
The phrase "because it is like space" illustrates this through analogy.
Since the true Dharma is free from marks and resembles the great void of the world, it is said to be "like space."
The following line concludes the preceding discussion on the transcendence of names.
"Dharmas are without conceptual proliferation" (niṣprapañca) precisely clarifies that the principle itself is without [proliferation].
Since names and phrases outside of the principle constitute conceptual proliferation, being free from these within the reality (tattva) is what is meant by "being without conceptual proliferation."
By this, he concludes the preceding point regarding the meaning of being "beyond names," and thus says they are "without conceptual proliferation.
The phrase "because of ultimate emptiness" explains this by revealing its absence.
To be forever severed from verbal discourse is called ultimate emptiness.
The above has explained how phenomena are devoid of characteristics with respect to the aggregates (*skandha*).
From here on, secondly, it explains how phenomena are devoid of characteristics with respect to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The six sense organs, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses constitute the eighteen elements.
In this passage, there are nineteen distinct sections:
the first section clarifies the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), while the subsequent eighteen sections clarify the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
Within the first section, the phrase "there is no 'mine' in phenomena" specifically clarifies the absence of intrinsic reality (*tattva-abhāva*).
In the luminous True Dharma, there is no self (*ātman*) nor anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*); the meaning is as explained above.
Regarding the phrase "because of being free from what belongs to a self," this is an explanation used to manifest non-existence.
Although there are eighteen phrases within the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), they are grouped into three according to their characteristics:
The first six phrases clarify the emptiness of the six sense organs;
the five phrases beginning with "dharmas are without movement" clarify the emptiness of the six consciousnesses;
and the seven phrases beginning with "dharmas are free from likes and dislikes" clarify the emptiness of the six sense objects.
Among the first six statements, the first three refute characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), while the latter three reveal reality (*tattva*).

Within the first three, the first statement clarifies the emptiness of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) by means of consciousness; the second demonstrates the emptiness of the sense-faculties by attaining their objects (*viṣaya*); and the third manifests the emptiness of the sense-faculties by means of the self (*ātman*).
Regarding the first phrase, "the dharmas are without discrimination," this correctly clarifies that there is no [subjective] principle.
Within the true Dharma, there are no six sense organs producing consciousness to cognize objects; this is termed "non-discrimination."
"Because it is detached from all consciousnesses" is explained to reveal its non-existence.
Within the scope of phenomenal objects, the six sense organs give rise to consciousness;
since this does not exist within the ultimate truth (*tattva*), it is called "detached from all consciousnesses."
Because it is free from all consciousnesses, there is no discrimination.
In the second phrase, "dharmas have no comparison," this precisely clarifies that the principle is without comparison;
for the mutual confrontation of sense-faculties and objects is what is termed "comparison."
In true reality, these do not exist; this is called the incomparability of phenomena (*dharma-asamāna*).
The phrase "the absence of mutual dependence" explains this by revealing its non-existence.
Because there is no mutual conditioning between sense organs and their objects, it is described as incomparable.
In the third phrase, "dharmas do not belong to causes," this precisely clarifies that there is no such thing as a principle [of causality].
Within the scope of conventional phenomena (*saṃvṛti*), when the sense faculties arise from causes and act as effects for those causes, it is called "belonging to causes.
In the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), this does not exist; thus, it is said they "do not belong to causes."
Regarding the phrase "because it does not exist as a condition," this is explained to demonstrate its non-existence.
That which produces directly is called a cause (*hetu*); that which assists indirectly is termed a condition (*pratyaya*).
If a condition were present, one could then speak of its belonging to a specific cause in relation to it.
Since there can be no "condition" (pratyaya) present, against what could one know that it is said to "belong to a cause" (hetu)?

Furthermore, "condition" may be a synonym for "cause"; thus, when it is said that [the effect] does not exist in the condition, one should know that this is simply saying it does not exist in the cause. It is impossible to state repeatedly to clarify its non-existence in the condition.
Birth is not separate from conditions; because of them, it exists.
Truth does not rely on conditions; therefore, it is said not to exist [in that sense].
Because it does not exist within conditions, it simply does not belong to causes.

In the latter three phrases, the identity with reality (*tattva*) is revealed by means of the three repositories: suchness (*tathatā*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
How do these three differ?

Within true dharmas, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is termed "suchness"; that which has names is termed the "dharma-nature"; and that which is neither existent nor non-existent is called the "limit of reality."
In what sense is true suchness empty?
It is empty because it is devoid of characteristics and devoid of intrinsic nature.
In what sense is it not empty?
It is endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
Why, then, is it called neither existent nor non-existent?
Existence and non-existence are of one and the same essence.

The meaning of this suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is explained extensively in other chapters and should be discussed here in full detail.

Since the true Dharma revealed herein shares the same essence as these three gateways while being distinguished by their functional aspects, one may speak of the Dharma as being identical to suchness, the nature of phenomena, the limit of reality, and so forth.
Regarding the first phrase, "the dharmas are identical to the dharma-nature" (dharmāḥ samānā dharmatayā), this is correctly explained according to their characteristics.

Within the Tathāgatagarbha, all Buddha-dharmas are termed "dharma-nature"; the true dharma being elucidated is of one essence with that [dharma-nature], and because they are one and not different, they are said to be "identical."
In what sense is it said that the *dharmatā* is identical?
The *dharmatā* is pure, eternal, and unchanging; that which is discerned is likewise so, and for this reason it is said to be identical.
The phrase "because it enters into all phenomena" explains this by revealing its identity.
"Entering" (ru) is synonymous with "conforming" (shun).
Because one conforms to the nature of all phenomena (dharmatā), it is called "sameness" (tong).
How is this single essence (ekātmya-dharma) described as conforming?
What is meant by "entering"?
Although their essential nature is one, the gates of meaning are always distinct.
Because the meanings differ while the essence remains the same, it is called "entering."
The same applies to all subsequent sections.
In the second clause, "the dharma conforms to suchness" (*tathatā*), this correctly distinguishes the characteristic itself as being non-different from the meaning of suchness.
Although the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is distinct, the principle of emptiness is not different; therefore, it is called "suchness."
The dharmas being analyzed accord with that [reality] in accordance with reason; therefore, they are called "conforming" (anuloma).
One might ask: since these [dharmas] are identical to that [reality], how can they be said to "conform" to it?
The meaning is as explained previously: because the specific gates differ while the underlying meaning remains the same, it is appropriate to speak of them as "conforming."
The preceding passage follows this same principle; the words "left and right" are used for illustration.
The phrase "because there is nothing to follow" explains the meaning of "following.
Since there is no following with respect to existing phenomena (*bhāva*), one accords with suchness (*tathatā*).
In the third phrase, "the Dharma abides in the limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*), the characteristics are correctly explained.
"Limit" (*koṭi*) refers to a boundary; it is a specific designation for a location.
The point where reality is exhausted is called the "limit of reality."
The true Dharma thus discerned is precisely the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); this is termed "abiding.
The preceding phrase "following this abiding" refers merely to its vicinity.
The expression "immovable from all extremes" explains and establishes the meaning of abiding.
Because one is not swayed by the two extremes of existence and non-existence, one abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
The subsequent five phrases clarify consciousness within emptiness: the first two refute characteristics, while the latter three reveal the reality itself.

Within the first two phrases, the initial one clarifies the emptiness of consciousness by way of its objects, while the subsequent phrase clarifies emptiness directly with respect to the substance of consciousness itself.
Regarding the first phrase, "dharmas are without movement," this precisely clarifies the non-existence of [intrinsic] principle.
The mind of the six consciousnesses comes and goes to grasp sensory objects; this is called "wavering.
The true Dharma is eternally abiding and is not like that; thus it is called "non-wavering.
The phrase "not relying on the six sense-objects" explains this by revealing its non-existence.
Because it does not arise together with the six consciousnesses and the six sense objects, it is without movement or fluctuation.
Within the latter phrase, "dharmas have no coming or going," this precisely clarifies that the principle is non-existent.
The mind of the six consciousnesses flows through the three periods of time, which is termed "going and coming"; "going" refers to the past and "coming" refers to the future.
True Dharma is not like this, and therefore it has no going or coming.
"Because it does not abide constantly" explains and establishes [the point].
That which is present is called "abiding"; if true dharmas had ever abided in the present, then one could speak of their going and coming in relation to them.
Since dharmas have no present abiding, knowing what could one look toward to speak of going or coming?
These two [terms] dispel characteristics; the following three are the reality itself, namely the three gates of liberation.
The meaning of these three gates of liberation will be explained as follows.
"Conforming to emptiness" means conforming to the gate of emptiness.
"Following signlessness" means following the gate of signlessness.
"Responding to wishlessness" means responding to the gate of wishlessness.
"Conforming" (*anuloma*) comes first, "following" (*ānugama*) next, and "corresponding" (*anuvartana*) is explained last; "ornamented speech" (*prapañca*) is merely a synonym for these as well.
Furthermore, because the True Dharma shares the same essence as these three gates despite differing in meaning, it is possible to speak of conforming, following, and corresponding.

Regarding the latter seven phrases that clarify the emptiness of the objective realm (*viṣaya*), there are four initial phrases that directly explain its emptiness by means of the very substance of the realm;
next, one phrase distinguishes emptiness with respect to the sense faculties (*indriya*);
and finally, one further phrase again explains the substance of the realm to demonstrate its emptiness.
The final phrase discusses emptiness in relation to consciousness.
Within the first four [phrases], "Dharma is free from beauty and ugliness" clarifies being free from the marks of sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
Within the scope of phenomenal things, objects possess qualities of excellence or deficiency; these are termed "good" and "bad," or "beautiful" and "ugly."
Since the true Dharma does not possess these [characteristics], it is said to be "detached.
The phrase "the Dharma has neither increase nor decrease" clarifies the functioning of the Dharma that is detached from objects.
That which accords with and benefits is called "increase," while that which opposes and hinders is collectively termed "decrease."
The true Dharma transcends these; thus it is said to be without increase or decrease.
"Dharmas have no arising or ceasing; dharmas have no place of return" clarifies that they are detached from the substance of the six sense-objects.
The substance of the six sense-objects has arising and perishing, which is termed "arising and ceasing"; when this pertains to persons, it is called "returning."
In the true Dharma, these do not exist; therefore, there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor is there any place of return.
This concludes the first section.
As for the statement, "The Dharma transcends the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind," this clarifies the emptiness of the sense objects in relation to the six faculties.
Within the limits of conventional phenomena, the six sense objects are the domains of the six sense organs and are not considered "transgressions";
however, within ultimate reality, there are no sense objects, and since the organs and so forth do not reach them, they are termed "transgressions."
These two sections are concluded.
Regarding the phrase "dharmas have no high or low," this again examines the substance of the objects (*viṣaya*) to distinguish their emptiness.

Within the limits of phenomenal reality, objects possess degrees of excellence or inferiority: the objects of the higher stages (*bhūmi*) are superior and are termed "high," while the objects of the lower stages are inferior and are described as "low."
The true Dharma transcends these, and therefore there is no high or low.
"Permanently abiding and immovable" explains the absence of high and low.
This concludes the three sections.
"The Dharma is apart from contemplative practice" distinguishes emptiness in terms of consciousness.
Within the limits of phenomenal objects, sensory objects serve as conditions for consciousness and do not depart from contemplative practice;
however, within the true Dharma, there are no objects to be conditioned, and for this reason it is said to be "apart from all contemplative practice."
The above constitutes the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*).
Regarding the phrase, "How can such characteristics of phenomena be spoken?", this is a reprimand by way of reason.
It restates what was previously analyzed, naming it "the phenomena are thus" (*dharmatā tathā*).
Since names and marks are utterly severed and mental activities are likewise non-existent, how could they be proclaimed?
Thus far, the teaching has proceeded by way of that which is spoken;
next, the teaching proceeds by way of that which is capable of speaking.
Within this, he first teaches the abandonment of four kinds of mind; "thereafter" refers to the concluding exhortation to proclaim [the teaching].
What are these four minds?
First, the teaching to eliminate the mind of views.
2. From "One should understand" downward, he teaches the abandonment of the deluded mind;
3. With "By means of great compassion," he does not teach the relinquishing of the small mind;
4. From "Mindful of repaying kindness" downward, he teaches the distancing from the ordinary mind.
Within the first phrase, the teaching commands one to distance oneself from the retribution of "self" and "person," which is called "removing the mind of views.
Regarding this, the instruction is first given through a Dharma-exposition:
"The one who preaches the Dharma neither speaks nor demonstrates," clarifying that there is no person who speaks.
To speak in relation to the Dharma is called "explaining";
to speak in relation to persons is termed "indicating.
Since, in ultimate reality, these do not exist, it is called "neither explaining nor indicating."
The statement "one who hears the Dharma has no attainment" clarifies that there is no person who hears.
When "hearing" is contrasted with "speech," it is termed "listening";
when "about to hear" is contrasted with "the Dharma," it is described as "attainment."
In principle, it also does not exist; this is called "attainment through non-hearing.
Next, the meaning is clarified by means of a simile:
"For example, like a phantom person" serves as a metaphor for the absence of a speaker.
"To preach for an illusory person" is a metaphor for having no listener.
"One should establish" and below is the exhortation.
In the second phrase, teaching the Dharma of the faculties (*indriya*) before initiating the discourse is called being free from deluded mind.
"When one has fully understood that the faculties of sentient beings are either sharp or dull," this is an exhortation to know the faculties (*indriya*).
Because Maudgalyāyana had previously preached in a way that did not accord with their capacities, he was exhorted to understand their faculties.
"Being skilled in knowing and seeing what constitutes an obstruction" encourages the knowledge of the Dharma.
Because Maudgalyāyana’s previous statement was not in accord with principle, he is thus encouraged to know the Dharma.
In the third phrase, he is taught to cultivate a broad mind; teaching the generation of a great intention is called "abandoning the narrow mind."
"By means of great compassion" teaches the cultivation of a vast mind.
To contemplate sentient beings extensively is called great compassion.
"Praising the Mahāyāna" teaches the generation of the great mind.
Because the mind is great, one praises the Mahāyāna.
In the fourth phrase, the instruction to abandon the demonic activities and heterodox studies of non-Buddhists is called "distancing oneself from the mundane mind.
The phrase "mindful of repaying the Buddha's kindness" teaches the abandonment of demonic activities.
To seek benefit from the Buddha's Dharma while simultaneously wishing to cause it harm is called betraying the Buddha's kindness.
Conversely, for a bodhisattva to maintain the intention to protect the Dharma is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
"Never severing the Three Jewels" teaches one to distance oneself from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Non-Buddhists practice false vehicles and contravene the True Dharma; this is called "severing the Three Jewels.

In contrast, the Bodhisattva personally seeks the True Dharma and teaches it to others, enabling the Three Jewels to continue in succession without interruption; therefore, this is called "never severing the Three Jewels."
The above constitutes the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*).
"Thereupon he preached the Dharma" serves as a general conclusion and exhortation.
The above is the second section, clarifying the words of admonition.
The third [point] concerns the benefit of the teaching, and the fourth concerns Maudgalyāyana’s own inferiority and deficiency; these are clear from the text and may be understood accordingly.
The former constitutes the statement of the request, while the latter provides the explanation.
“Therefore, I am not fit” summarizes his inability to undertake the task.

First, in response to Śāriputra, the Dharma of non-abiding is clarified; next, in response to Maudgalyāyana, the Dharma of realization is clarified; finally, in response to four individuals, the Dharma of auxiliary practices is clarified.
Within this, the initial pair—Kāśyapa and Subhūti—is used to clarify the practice of begging for food, which subsumes the Dharma of merit;
the subsequent pair—Pūrṇa and Kātyāyana—is used to clarify the practice of entering the Dharma, which subsumes the Dharma of wisdom.
Regarding the first two [sections], the former addresses Kāśyapa to clarify the method of begging for food, while the latter addresses Subhūti to clarify the method of receiving food.

Regarding the latter two [sections], the former addresses Pūrṇa to clarify the method of setting out on the journey, while the latter addresses Kātyāyana to clarify the method of generating understanding.
The explanation is thus.
Previously, Kāśyapa was instructed to inquire after the Dharma regarding his illness.
Kāśyapa is his clan name; his personal name is Mahāprajāpatī, which is translated here as "Great Benefactor. He was the elder sister of the Buddha.
“Mahā” means great; “dāna” means giving; and “pāramitā” is termed the foremost.
He was of the brāhmaṇa caste in the city of Rājagṛha, born into an extremely wealthy and noble family, and his wife’s name was Vāsavadattā.

In the past, during the time of the Buddha Viśvabhū, this person was a master image-maker. At that time, there was a woman who commissioned this image-maker to construct a Buddha image, providing him with one golden bracelet.

By virtue of this merit and goodness, they have constantly encountered one another; now, having met in the age of a Buddha, they have once again become husband and wife, their bodies both golden in color.
Remaining free from desire even while in the secular world, they together left the household life and equally attained the state of Arhatship.
The details of these events are as described in the sutra.
Among the Buddha’s disciples, Kāśyapa was foremost in the practice of dhūta; he constantly went on almsround.
Now, as you are summoned to inquire after his illness, I shall first instruct you to go and inquire after his health.
The term "Kāśyapa" occurs frequently; here, the most prominent one is used as the designation.
The subsequent phrasing expresses an inability [to accept].
Within this, the first part provides a general summary; the section beginning with "Therefore" offers an explanation; and the section beginning with "For this reason" provides the conclusion.
In the commentary on the phrase "the reason why," following the self-interrogation that has arisen, the subsequent section provides a detailed explanation.
This text is divided into three parts:
first, citing the circumstances by which [the Buddha] was rebuked in the past; [the other two parts follow].
2. From "At that time, Vimalakīrti... onwards, the words of reprimand are presented;

3. From "At that time, World-Honored One, having heard this being said... onwards, [the narrator] personally reveals his own inferiority and deficiency, thereby manifesting the opponent's invincibility.
The opening section, "Recalling the Past," introduces the occasion of being rebuked.
"Begging in a poor neighborhood" brings forth the specific matter for which he was rebuked.

Kāśyapa’s intention was this: he felt pity for those who were poor and lacked merit; seeing that they currently experienced poverty as a result of past actions, he now sought alms from them with the desire that they might become wealthy in the future. Therefore, he begged in a poor neighborhood.
Because of this inequality, he was subsequently rebuked.
From here begins the second section: Vimalakīrti’s instruction and rebuke. Why must this be so?
In order to cause Kāśyapa to abandon the minor and embrace the major, he was thus instructed and rebuked.
In the text, "Vimalakīrti came and said" serves as the general introduction;
what follows below provides the specific details, among which the initial section constitutes the rebuke.
"Abiding in the dharma of equality, one should act accordingly" is the exhortation.
Within the censure, the initial statement, "Though possessing a heart of compassion, one is unable to be universal," constitutes the actual censure.
To abandon the wealthy and follow the poor is an act that lacks universality;
it is an instance of non-universal conduct. Furthermore, the preceding phrase is criticized because its lack of compassion violates the Bodhisattva’s universal compassion;
abandoning the wealthy and following the poor is criticized because it violates the sequential begging prescribed within the dhūta practices.
Within the instruction, there are three parts:
first, the formal instruction on begging for food, which is termed "the mind of begging";
second, from the passage beginning with "as an empty village" onwards, the instruction regarding the proper conduct and the avoidance of faults during the time of begging for food.
Third, from "If one is able not to abandon the eight heterodoxies" onwards, the teaching on generating the dharmas of the Path follows the practice of begging for food.
Within the preceding section, the four phrases do not follow a sequential order based on their subject matter.
To discuss these in sequence: begging for alms is first; begging a second time is next; taking [the food] is third; and receiving it is fourth.
However, in the present text, because the purpose is to provide instruction on begging a second time for the sake of benefiting others, it is discussed first.
The act of begging and the subsequent taking [of what is given] constitute "receiving"; because this teaches self-benefit, it is discussed later.
Furthermore, obtaining [alms] next to begging teaches the abandonment of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) and the overcoming of their faults; therefore, it is discussed first.
The acts of begging and subsequently taking what is received are both taught as the abandonment of the faults of ordinary birth-and-death (saṃsāra); therefore, they are discussed later.
Regarding the first point, "begging within the state of equality," this teaches the cultivation of an impartial mind, correcting the previous inability to extend compassion universally.

Regarding the second point, "one should beg in succession," this teaches the cultivation of impartial conduct, correcting the previous practice of abandoning wealthy areas to beg only in poor neighborhoods.
In the latter three phrases, this teaching is self-evident, as there is both implicit and explicit meaning.

The first phrase states that one must practice begging for food in order to distance oneself from the conditions of birth and death; the second states that one must take morsel food in order to sever the causes of birth and death; and the third states that one must accept that food in order to abandon the fruits of birth and death.

Regarding the first sentence, "One should practice begging for the sake of non-eating": food is a condition for the body; only when one attains the pure Dharma-body can one truly relinquish and distance oneself from it.

That pure Dharma-body must be cultivated by abandoning worldly activities for the sake of livelihood; it can only be attained by begging for food to sustain the body while practicing the Way. Therefore, one must practice begging without eating [of ordinary food].

In the second sentence, regarding the phrase "one should take food for the sake of destroying the composite": because causes can aggregate to produce effects, they are termed "composite"; it is only upon internally realizing the True Path that one is forever separated from them.

That path must necessarily involve relinquishing worldly requisites for life; one can only realize the truth by undertaking practice while sustaining the body through food obtained from others. Therefore, this constitutes the breaking of the corresponding attachment to edible food that is gathered through social combination.
From the moment he requested it, it was then called "taking.

Regarding the phrase "one should accept food for the sake of non-acceptance": that which does not accept the conditioned fruits of birth and death is termed "non-acceptance"; such non-acceptance belongs exclusively to the Buddha.

The fruit of Buddhahood arises from two factors: the renunciation of worldly glory and the acceptance of sustenance for the body from others in order to give rise to the Path; thus, one who does not accept [offerings] must nevertheless receive that food.
Only when he has received it from the one who bestows it is it called "acceptance.
Below this is the second instruction on the ritual for preventing transgressions:
"Entering a village with the perception of an empty hamlet" means that at the time of entering a village, one is instructed to abandon the perception of people.
Because one observes that the aggregates are devoid of a person, they are termed "empty.
Because many fetters, such as those of male and female, arise upon entering a village, the practice of emptiness is taught.
From the passage "the forms seen," etc., the teaching is given to abandon the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*) during the time of begging for alms.
When begging for alms, many fetters arise in relation to the six sense objects; therefore, he teaches the prevention of them and detachment from them.

However, within this text, the remedial methods for the six sensory objects differ: regarding the object of visible form, he teaches the contemplation of the emptiness of the sense faculty as the remedy; regarding the object of sound, he teaches the contemplation of the unreality of the object as the remedy; regarding the object of odor, he teaches the categorization of coarse phenomena as the remedy; regarding the object of taste, he teaches the relinquishing of the grasping mind as the remedy; regarding the object of touch, he teaches the relinquishing of both the subject that grasps and the object that is grasped as the remedy; and regarding the object of mental phenomena, he teaches the contemplation of the emptiness of the object as the remedy.

All are attained by following [the teaching]; this is established as a summary for those who mostly practice according to these six teachings, clarifying the differences between manifest and hidden doctrines.
Regarding the initial statement, "Seeing forms is equal to being blind," it means that a blind person lacks the sense organ and thus does not become attached to forms.
The practitioner should act accordingly: they should contemplate that the essence of the eye is empty, like a blind person who lacks the faculty and thus does not grasp at forms.
Therefore, the text below states: "If one knows the nature of the eye, one will have no greed, hatred, or delusion regarding forms"; the same applies to the other [senses].
Regarding the statement that "the sounds one hears are like echoes," an echo is empty and non-existent, and thus nothing can be grasped or craved therein.
One should contemplate that sounds are likewise illusory and unreal, resembling that echo, and thus nothing can be grasped or craved therein; the same applies to all other things as well.
Regarding the statement "the odors smelled are equal to the wind," since the substance of wind is light and coarse, people generally do not become attached to it.
Contemplate that the odors are like it and do not give rise to craving or attachment; this should apply to all other cases as well.
Regarding the statement, "one does not discriminate among the flavors one eats," this indicates that the ladle is mindless; although it is amidst various flavors, it gives rise to no discrimination.
A practitioner should be like this: they should, like the ladle, eliminate mental conceptions and not give rise to discrimination; all else should be treated in the same way.

Regarding the statement, "Experiencing various contacts is like the realization of fragrance": when wisdom realizes phenomena, one does not perceive one's own mind as the grasper, nor does one perceive the external object as the grasped.

The practitioner should act thus: knowing that the body is empty and lacks any capacity for cognition, and observing that objects are empty and lack anything to be cognized; therefore, as it is realized through wisdom, so it should be for all else as well.
"Knowing that phenomena are like illusions and lack the nature of self or other" teaches the contemplation of the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
An illusion has no fixed nature; likewise, all phenomena, being like these illusory things, have no essence, which is termed "lack of intrinsic nature."
Within these illusory phenomena, there is likewise no real self, person, or other such false conceptualizations; this is called the absence of other-nature (*parabhāva*).
"Originally not so, and now not extinguished" teaches the contemplation of the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
Just as the characteristics of the causal conditions of those illusory transformations are ultimately empty and quiescent— not only lacking intrinsic nature, but even their marks do not exist—
because they are markless, no dharma can arise, and thus they were never ignited from the beginning;
because no dharma can be extinguished, they are not now extinguished.
Furthermore, knowing that all is like an illusion clarifies that phenomena are not non-existent.
The absence of self-nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth reveals that phenomena are not existent; the absence of both self-nature and other-nature clarifies that they do not exist as intrinsic natures.
Being fundamentally non-arisen, they are likewise unextinguished, clarifying that they do not exist as characteristics.
The meaning is as explained previously.
Furthermore, "knowing that phenomena have an illusory nature" clearly indicates the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
"the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and so forth" clearly indicates the understanding of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The absence of self and other-nature is the True Truth of the Emptiness of Nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
That which was originally not so is now likewise not extinguished; this is the True Truth of the Emptiness of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
These are also explained as above.
Since the contemplation of phenomena is thus established, other sensory objects are likewise treated in this manner.
The preceding section was the second, which taught the proper etiquette for guarding against faults during the time of begging for food.
From here on is the third section, which teaches the methods for generating the Path during the time of consuming the food obtained through begging.
There are ten distinct sections:

the first three sections establish the Path through the direct teaching; the middle five sections manifest the benefits and exhort practice; and the final two sections praise its excellence and exhort study.
Among the aforementioned three, the first two teach the practice of benefiting others, while the last one teaches the practice of benefiting oneself.
Furthermore, within the first two, the instruction "not abandoning the eight wrong paths while entering the eight liberations" is taught in terms of the cause.
The śrāvaka seeks solitary excellence; therefore, he abandons the eight heterodoxies to enter the eight liberations.
The bodhisattva benefits both self and others; appearing in conformity with sentient beings, he does not abandon the eight heterodoxies before entering the eight liberations.

Regarding the "eight wrongs" (*aṣṭa-mithyā*): they are spoken of as the counterparts to the eight right paths; namely, wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, and so forth, up to wrong concentration.

Regarding the "eight liberations": from one perspective, those same eight right paths are called the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), because those eight stand in opposition to the wrong and the right.

Furthermore, those states such as "possessing internal perception of form while externally perceiving forms" may also be called the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), because one cultivates them to counteract the fault of craving for food.

Therefore, the text below says: "The Buddha has taught the eight liberations; you, O noble one, should accept and practice them. How could you listen to the Dharma while being preoccupied with the desire for food?"
Therefore, when it is taught among humans that "one enters the True Dharma by means of false appearances," this is taught in terms of the fruit.

False appearances refer to the mundane world and the True Dharma refers to Nirvana; the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas abandon the false and enter the true for their own individual liberation, whereas Bodhisattvas benefit both themselves and others, manifesting in conformity with sentient beings as they encounter them.
Without abandoning the world, one realizes nirvana; thus, without abandoning what is erroneous, one enters the True Dharma.
